item.title: CNMI delegate urges path forward as DHS halts Chinese travel program

item.content:encoded:
Emphasizing that the program has been "suspended, not terminated," CNMI Del. Kimberlyn King-Hinds said Tuesday she is working with federal officials to address concerns that prompted the suspension of a key travel program for Chinese visitors to the Northern Mariana Islands.

King-Hinds said she spoke directly with the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and House leadership following the Department of Homeland Security's announcement suspending the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, or EVS-TAP. She said Mullin assured her that DHS would work directly with the CNMI to better understand and address the issues that led to the suspension.

King-HInds said, "We have experienced interruptions to travel programs serving the Commonwealth before, and we will work through this together with our federal partners to address the concerns that have been raised and find a path forward, just as we have done before."

According to the delegate, the program was established with safeguards allowing DHS to suspend operations when security or law enforcement concerns arise. She said federal and local officials would work together to address those concerns and support the program's resumption as quickly as possible.

The congresswoman also warned that a lengthy suspension could further burden the Commonwealth's struggling tourism sector.

"Our tourism industry is already facing tremendous challenges, and a prolonged disruption would have serious consequences for our businesses, workers and families," King-Hinds said. "We must also consider the immediate effects on airlines, travel arrangements, and the businesses that depend on visitor arrivals."

The Department of Homeland Security announced Tuesday that it will suspend EVS-TAP effective Oct. 30, requiring Chinese nationals seeking to visit the CNMI for business or tourism to obtain a U.S. visa unless another lawful exception applies.

Chinese nationals already admitted under the program may remain through their authorized period of stay.

In a Federal Register notice, DHS said the program's suspension was warranted because of national security, immigration enforcement and law enforcement concerns. The agency cited the risk of unauthorized travel beyond the CNMI, potential espionage activities involving sensitive military infrastructure in the Mariana Islands, birth tourism concerns and previous criminal cases involving the smuggling of Chinese nationals from the CNMI to Guam.

EVS-TAP took effect in February 2025 and allowed pre-screened nationals of the People's Republic of China to travel directly to the CNMI without first obtaining a U.S. visa. More than 3,000 Chinese nationals used the program during fiscal year 2025, according to DHS.

While acknowledging that some CNMI businesses have relied on Chinese tourism, DHS said economic considerations do not outweigh what it described as acute national security, immigration and law enforcement concerns. The agency noted that Chinese visitors may still travel to the CNMI through the standard U.S. visa process.

King-Hinds said her immediate focus is ensuring the concerns identified by federal officials are addressed so the program can resume.

item.content:encoded:
National Weather Service forecasters are watching Typhoon In-fa, located about 1,200 miles east of Guam, which is expected to pass through the Northern Islands as a major typhoon on Friday.

On Monday afternoon, forecasters said In-Fa could be undergoing a period of rapid intensification.

The Joint Typhoon Warning Center put the storm’s closest point of approach to Saipan at 150 miles, which was still within the cone of uncertainty.

Officials advised people in the CNMI not to let their guard down, because any shift to the south over the coming days could bring strong winds and heavy rain closer to Saipan and Tinian.

item.content:encoded:
Housing shortages, strained infrastructure, and environmental safety were among the major concerns raised during a Guam Legislature informational briefing on the military buildup.

Sen. Telo Taitague hosted the briefing, the fourth one held during the current legislative term. She said shifting federal priorities and regional security developments could change the scope of the buildup, potentially placing additional pressure on Guam’s housing supply, utility systems, and cost of living.

Written testimony from Community Defense Liaison Office Executive Director Vera Topasna said local planning accounts for approximately 5,000 Marines relocating to Guam, with peak buildup activity projected between 2027 and 2037. The timeline remains subject to change.

Former Del. Robert Underwood said the public needs more detailed information about military plans and their potential effects on the island. He questioned whether local needs are adequately reflected in decisions made at the federal level.

Environmental concerns were also raised by community members.

Testimony submitted by Baltazar Bordallo Aguon and read by his nephew, Tomas Aguon Rojas, questioned the handling of potentially contaminated soil and raised concerns about dieldrin in groundwater. He also questioned the environmental risks associated with open-air detonation of expired munitions.

Claire Calvo, founder of Conscious Living, called for independent environmental monitoring and long-term health research to better understand potential cumulative exposures and their possible relationship to health outcomes.

“When we inhale or ingest toxins, particles, and chemicals, substances can enter the bloodstream and be processed or eliminated through organs, including the liver and kidneys,” Calvo said. “These correlations deserve to be explored in the broader investigation of Guam's environmental exposures. We've often been led to look towards our genetics, diet, and lifestyle as explanations for our health disparities, and those factors should definitely not be disregarded. But neither should our environment.”

The discussion also addressed whether federal investment will adequately support Guam’s civilian infrastructure as military activity expands. Written testimony from Del. James Moylan discussed proposed funding for power-grid upgrades, housing construction, and Port Authority improvements.

Military representatives from Joint Region Marianas, Moylan, and the governor’s liaison, Vera Topasna, did not attend the briefing to answer questions directly. Sens. Taitague and Chris Barnett were the only senators in attendance.

Taitague said she would continue seeking testimony from military and government agencies and recessed the hearing to a later date.

The briefing left questions about the buildup’s long-term effects, environmental safeguards, and infrastructure needs unresolved.

item.title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
item.description: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment. item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.

The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections.

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."

The Justice Department said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the statute of limitations for when they can permissibly bring an indictment.

"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.

An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury's finding of probable cause to a court. Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by a 10-year statute of limitations.

"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI's conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said.

Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey "sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns "and thereby illegally transferred classified information."

The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 6, 2016, 10 years after the story was published. "But," Comey's lawyers said, "the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice."

They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

The cases are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey's daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey's firing. Comey in 2018 published a memoir, "A Higher Loyalty," that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him "untethered to truth." Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for "treason" — an accusation Comey dismissed as "dumb lies" — and called him an "untruthful slime ball."

item.title: Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud
item.description: In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars , the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards. In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from
item.content:encoded:
In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars , the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.

In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.

Many banks in the U.S. took action against this issue over a decade ago by upgrading their cards to include microchips and tap-to-pay, which are considered more secure. But states have lagged in making such a transition for Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, which are what SNAP recipients use to access food aid. Currently, fewer than a third of states have made the switch or are in process of doing so, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Now, under the proposed rule released by the USDA last week, all states would have to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards. It also requires retailers that accept SNAP benefits to have payment terminals that support tap-pay. The USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, which administers SNAP, attributed card skimming as a reason behind the proposal.

"These proposed changes will protect SNAP benefits from thieves and ensure benefits are accessible by approved households," the Food and Nutrition Administration said in its summary of the rule.

Back in January, the USDA Office of Inspector General projected that SNAP theft could climb to $233 million between 2025 and 2026 — largely as a result of skimming. A recent ProPublica investigation found that last year, $470 million was stolen electronically from SNAP recipients. The total was calculated using data from Propel, an app that helps SNAP recipients check their food benefits.

In most states, stolen benefits are not replaced — leaving recipients to make difficult choices, such as skipping meals or borrowing money in order to pay for groceries, according to Propel .

Earlier this month, NPR reported that food assistance card modernization had widespread support from state officials and federal watchdogs, as well as Republicans and Democrats in Congress. But money has been a major barrier for states to make the switch. According to the Government Accountability Office, chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than their magnetic strip counterparts.

The federal push for stronger card security features comes as state SNAP agencies are facing new budget pressures triggered by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The proposed regulation recognized the financial barrier, adding that the USDA is interested in hearing from state agencies about the cost burden.

"As stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits," the proposed rule said.

The public has 60 days to submit comments on the proposal before the USDA publishes a final rule. The department is considering giving states a two-year deadline from that publication date to implement the rule, but it also welcomed input on whether that's enough time.

When asked if the department would consider providing funding to help states upgrade their card technology, the USDA said that "For years, States had access to administrative funds to stop this egregious abuse of taxpayer resources. Yet few acted."

The USDA added that the proposed rule has been in the works for nearly four years. It estimates that the changes will reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade.

SNAP has been one of the focus areas in the Trump administration's war on fraud. Last week, the Justice Department announced that its fraud division helped uncover nearly $42 million in schemes targeting food benefits. The investigations ranged from identity theft to retailers illegally exchanging cash for food benefits.

item.title: Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey
item.description: A New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former prosecutor Maurene Comey, who is the daughter of ex-FBI Director James Comey . Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade, working on high-profile cases against defendants like Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Trump Justice Department fired her
item.content:encoded:
A New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former prosecutor Maurene Comey, who is the daughter of ex-FBI Director James Comey .

Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade, working on high-profile cases against defendants like Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Trump Justice Department fired her in July 2025 despite her consistently receiving accolades from the department for her work.

In response, she sued the Justice Department and others, arguing that her dismissal was unlawful and unconstitutional. Her lawsuit said she was fired because her father is the former FBI director, a prominent critic of President Trump.

The Justice Department has twice indicted the elder Comey. The first case was dismissed. The second prosecution, which is still pending, accuses him of threatening the president in a photo of seashells posted on social media.

In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman, a nominee of former President Barack Obama, wrote that the Department of Justice " invented a new and expansive theory of executive power " in dismissing Maurene Comey, and violated her constitutional right to due process.

"To accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," the judge wrote.

The opinion adds to concerns of politically motivated dismissals at the DOJ. Several federal prosecutors and former FBI agents have sued the DOJ under the Trump administration over their dismissals, alleging that they were fired for political reasons tied to their work.

Comey's lawyers praised Monday's ruling, and said it reaffirms that the president must comply with the law as part of the Constitution's checks and balances.

"This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," her attorneys said in a statement.

The judge's ruling calls for Comey to receive back pay dating to when she was fired last year, and for her to return as a prosecutor to the Southern District of New York, if she so chooses.

The Justice Department said it disagreed with the decision, and would appeal in due course.

The court's order is not final. Judge Furman did yet not rule on Maurene Comey's First Amendment argument that she was fired for politically protected speech, and plans to hear further briefings on that claim.

—With assistance from NPR's Carrie Johnson.

item.content:encoded:
I've been thinking a lot lately about the famous opening sequence of Up , the Pixar animated film. That movie begins with a wordless montage of a marriage, Carl and Ellie's marriage: its youthful giddiness, the pain of infertility and the long goodbye of Ellie's death in old age.

The montage takes less than four-and-a-half minutes and, yet, contains the emotional depths of a much longer film or novel about a marriage. Relying solely on words, Elizabeth McCracken 's Seven Stories About Tammy does much the same for the family saga.

As its title bluntly announces, Seven Stories About Tammy is composed of seven interrelated short stories about a family's encounters with their eldest son's girlfriend and eventual wife, an older woman named Tammy. McCracken's story sequence has appeared earlier in a literary magazine, as well as in the 2025 anthology of The Best American Short Stories . But, having it available in standalone book form is just the right vessel for this family montage. Not every piece of fiction, after all, fits into the prefab format of a novel or a single short story. The only downside is that this 70-page book is so tiny — the size of a pamphlet, really — that I misplaced it repeatedly around my house. Whenever I found it again, though, I felt like something rich and strange had been returned to me out of the jumble of the mundane.

We first meet Tammy when the Harkin family does: in the mid-1970s when eldest son, Morris, who's been living in Florida, brings her home to Boston for dinner. Here's our omniscient narrator describing that first encounter:

On that evening, the family "parlor game" of "how old is she?" will begin, because, we're flatly told: "Morris was twenty-seven. She wasn't."

In the third story, set about 15 years later, insecure middle child, Victoria, visits Tammy and Morris, now married, at their high-rise apartment in Philadelphia. Victoria, who's struggled with see-sawing weight all her young life, is served a shallow bowl of soup. Here's some dinner table dialogue:

What do we make of this moment? Is Tammy really a woman who, as Victoria thinks, "was never so happy as when other people were stupid"? Or is that a judgment born out of Victoria's own self-loathing?

Wielding precise-but-plain language, McCracken engages that central question of whether or not we ever really see ourselves or each other; twisting it like a helix, both within stories and throughout the long arc of this story sequence. In the penultimate story, the family (minus dad, Dennis, who's died) gathers at a rental house in Rhode Island for the holidays. Younger Harkin son, Porter, a recovering alcoholic, takes center stage here. Years ago, his drunken kiss of Tammy's shoulder on the night of her and Morris' wedding changed the course of Porter's life, or so goes the story he tells himself. Porter, naturally, blames Tammy for his diminished status in the family, the effort he has to make to be "picked up on the family radio."

However you categorize it, Seven Stories About Tammy is a brilliant piece of writing. This book is so funny, profound, and short that you may just want to read it over again, immediately, as I did.
